item.title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language.
item.abstract: Programming biological function-designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks-is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1-3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein-text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks-a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein-and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.

item.title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts.
item.abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1-5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6-8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

item.title: Generating protein hydrogels with customizable stress relaxation behavior via deep learning-driven entanglement design.
item.abstract: Protein hydrogels are promising artificial extracellular matrices (ECMs) for 3D stem cell and organoid culture due to their favorable stress relaxation behavior (a decrease in stress in response to strain). Inter-chain entangled motifs, in which different protein chains are interlaced, represent a powerful strategy to synthesize such hydrogels. However, designing these motifs with tailored properties such as binding energy remains a major challenge due to the difficulty of simultaneously controlling these properties while ensuring entanglement. Here, we introduce TangleDiff, a deep learning framework for the de novo design of homodimeric entangled proteins with programmable features. TangleDiff generates diverse foldable entangled sequences with an in-silico success rate exceeding 70%, markedly outperforming current models (~1%). By conditioning TangleDiff on inter-chain binding energy, we generate novel protein dimers whose binding energies closely match the specified ranges, with approximately 70% of successful designs conforming to expected values. We experimentally validate TangleDiff by designing nine homodimers targeting various binding energies; seven successfully form hydrogels, with stress relaxation dynamics correlated with specified binding energies. This work establishes a general strategy for entangled protein design, opening avenues for entanglement-based biomaterial innovation.

item.title: Genetic Biosensors for High-Throughput Biomedical Applications: Challenges and Advances.
item.abstract: Genetic biosensors represent a particularly promising class of bioengineered instruments designed to enable accurate, real-time monitoring of cellular and molecular processes, with especially strong relevance to high-throughput biomedical workflows. In this review, we provide a systematic, clearly structured overview of the field, covering the fundamental design principles that form the basis of today's platforms. We focus in particular on DNA-based, RNA-based, and CRISPR-based architectures while also examining engineered synthetic biology circuitry, and we place these foundational concepts in the context of more recent advances. These developments encompass improved sensitivity, increased scalability, and broader functionality for multiplexed detection. Beyond summarizing technological progress, we critically evaluate challenges that remain deeply embedded at both technical and biological levels, including limitations driven by signal-to-noise ratio constraints, practical difficulties in delivering probes into cells, and relatively restricted dynamic ranges. Taken together, these issues continue to hinder widespread, routine clinical adoption. Importantly, rather than presenting the topic only as a catalog of improvements, we argue for a unifying framework: the convergence of artificial intelligence and synthetic biology is actively reshaping biosensor engineering, moving it away from a largely empirical, trial-and-error approach toward a more reliable, data-driven discipline. To convert this conceptual shift into tangible outcomes, we also outline a practical implementation framework aimed at reducing the distance between research activities and real-world deployment. This framework emphasizes the need for scalable manufacturing processes, robust and reproducible clinical validation, and regulatory pathways capable of evolving as new evidence emerges. An integrated strategy of this kind is therefore essential for fully realizing the potential of real-time, multichannel biosensing platforms in both complex clinical diagnostics and point-of-care environments.

item.title: Innovative Microbial Chassis for Systems and Synthetic Biology.
item.abstract: The development of microbial chassis has revolutionized systems and synthetic biology, enabling the rational engineering of microorganisms for the biosynthesis of high-value metabolites ranging from pharmaceuticals to biofuels. This chapter systematically explores widely used and emerging microbial chassis systems, with a focus on their core biological characteristics, inherent advantages and limitations, cutting-edge advances in genetic and metabolic engineering, and real-world industrial application progress. Well-established chassis represented by Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae remain the gold standard mainstream platforms in both academic research and industrial production. Meanwhile, the growing global demand for sustainable, high-titer bioproduction has driven the development and application of functionally specialized industrial chassis including Bacillus subtilis and Corynebacterium glutamicum, which offer unique metabolic traits, exceptional environmental stress resistance, and broad substrate versatility. This chapter also discusses the core criteria for chassis selection, including genetic stability, industrial scalability, biosafety, and metabolic flexibility, alongside their validated applications in manufacturing a diverse array of products from bulk organic acids to complex biopharmaceuticals. By systematically comparing these chassis systems across key performance metrics, this chapter provides actionable insights into rational chassis design empowered by integrated systems and synthetic biology, to enable efficient, robust, and scalable biomanufacturing.

item.title: CEM 2.0: Co-evolution-guided mining of superior extremophilic proteins via a curated proteome database and protein language model.
item.abstract: Extremophilic proteins offer immense potential for diverse applications; however, their discovery is hindered by the reliance on predefined templates and domain-specific knowledge. Therefore, new methods are required to mine extremophilic proteins without relying on existing templates, enabling a comprehensive exploration of functional extremophilic proteins across the entire protein universe. Here, we propose a co-evolution-guided protein mining framework, CEM 2.0 (Co-Evolution Mining 2.0), comprising three synergistic components: (1) an extensive and diverse extremophilic proteome database covering six extremophilic features, (2) a multidimensional evaluator for six extremophilic features, leveraging the protein language model ProteinBERT, and (3) an integrated and interactive mining pipeline equipped with advanced tools for computing >20 properties of proteins. This framework was implemented on an interactive web platform (https://cem.sjtu.edu.cn/) equipped with intuitive visualization tools. We conducted wet-lab validation, performed a series of computational validations using published studies, and made recommendations for novel PETases, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness and potential of CEM 2.0 for the template-independent discovery of extremophilic proteins. CEM 2.0 is expected to mine functional extremophilic proteins across the protein universe in terms of evolutionary distance and serve as a valuable tool for protein engineering and synthetic biology.

item.title: Hierarchically Gated Multiplex Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network with Self-Distillation for Protein Stability Prediction.
item.abstract: Predicting the impact of protein residue mutations on thermal stability is critical for protein engineering and for understanding how mutations contribute to cancer development. Recent advances in deep learning demonstrate great promise in the prediction of mutation-induced protein stability changes; however, current approaches face several drawbacks to be solved: 1) neglect the inherent heterogeneity of relations among residues, 2) lack of information-filtering from noisy context, and 3) insufficient supervision of sparse and weak signals of mutation. To address these issues, we propose a protein stability prediction model named HierGate, which is featured by a hierarchically gated multiplex heterogeneous graph neural network with self-distillation mechanism. It is designed to capture the multiplex heterogeneous relations among residues; on the other hand, hierarchical gating mechanism is introduced to suppress contextual noise upon heterogeneous neighbor aggregation. In addition, self-distillation strategy is leveraged to amplify the weak mutation signal. Comprehensive evaluations on eight benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms advanced protein stability prediction approaches, with an improvement of up to 13% over the second-best baseline on certain datasets. We also demonstrate the practical capability of HierGate in investigating the underlying mechanisms of cancer development and in guiding directed evolution in protein engineering.

item.title: Base editing-mediated exon-specific knockout of glutamine synthetase generates a high-productivity CHO cell line for antibody manufacturing.
item.abstract: The Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell platform dominates recombinant protein production, with the glutamine synthetase (GS) system widely used for clonal selection. However, we observed variable performance between two commercial CHO lines (ATCC CHO-K1 and CHOZN®), which carry distinct intragenic GS deletions and differential residual transcript levels, raising the possibility that the premature termination codon (PTC) position contributes to this phenotypic divergence. To systematically assess the impact of the PTC position, we used base editing to introduce PTCs into each of the six coding exons of Glul. Among the resulting clonal lines, the exon 7-edited (E7) variant exhibited complete GS ablation and sustained high viability. In fed-batch production of an anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody, E7 achieved higher titers and specific productivities than CHOZN®, with sustained viability. Our findings demonstrate that PTC location is a key determinant of GS knockout completeness and cellular phenotype, identifying exon 7 as a critical knockout target that offers a defined, exon-resolved strategy for accelerating CHO cell line development and improving recombinant protein titers.

item.title: Assembly-Pathway Regulation Dictates pH-Responsive Actuation in the R-Body Protein Machinery.
item.abstract: Refractile bodies (R-bodies) are protein assemblies that form intracellular rolls and extend into spirals in response to environmental stimuli. Type 51 R-body assembles from four Reb proteins and undergoes rapid, repeatable ∼50-fold extension. Although R-bodies were described more than 70 years ago, the roles of RebC and RebD remained unclear, whereas RebA and RebB are proposed as major components. Here, we characterize the wild-type R-body (Rb_WT) and reb gene knockout mutants using integrated biophysical analyses. RebD was incorporated as a minor component, whereas RebC was not detectably incorporated into the final assembly. Mutants lacking RebA or RebB formed rolls but lost pH-dependent extension and the ordered lamellar architecture characteristic of Rb_WT. In contrast, mutants lacking RebC and/or RebD exhibited reduced roll formation and formed β-sheet-rich aggregation. Thus, pH-responsive actuation is dictated not simply by major architectural components alone, but by a regulated assembly pathway that builds the ordered lamellar architecture.

item.title: Structure of a sparsely populated chimeric intermediate that facilitates fold-switching of a metamorphic protein.
item.abstract: Metamorphic proteins challenge the single-sequence-structure-function paradigm by switching between distinct folds that often adopt complementary functions. However, the conformational states sampled along the fold-switching pathway have remained elusive because they are transient and unstable. Using multinuclear chemical exchange saturation transfer and relaxation dispersion NMR, combined with chemical shift-based structure determination and protein engineering, we visualized the atomic resolution structure of an "invisible" state of the metamorphic chemokine lymphotactin. This state is a chimera that integrates the secondary and tertiary structure of one fold with the quaternary assembly of the other. Locking lymphotactin into a single conformation abolishes access to this state, supporting its role as an on-pathway intermediate in metamorphosis. The stabilization of such hybrid intermediates is likely to have facilitated the evolution of fold-switching and represents a powerful strategy for protein design.

item.title: Engineering a Hyperstable Synthetic Miniprotein for B7-H3 Targeting.
item.abstract: Small protein ligands, such as miniproteins, have the potential to provide the efficient physiological transport and rapid clearance required for radioligand therapy. Yet, binders require single-digit nanomolar affinity for potent targeting and high stability for radiolabeling and physiological integrity. High affinity and stable single-domain miniproteins are also modular candidates for multispecific applications in cell engagers and avid constructs. Previous work demonstrated computationally designed 40-amino acid β⍺ββ miniproteins as effective scaffolds for ligand discovery. Herein, to yield the desired single-digit nanomolar affinity for B7-H3, an important immune regulator and cell surface antigen upregulated in numerous tumors, we used structural modeling to guide experimental evolution of the lead molecule. We performed constrained diversification at six sites on a β-sheet, structurally distinct from the originally engineered ⍺-helical paratope, as well as nine sites within the ⍺-helix, and sorted for strong binding to B7-H3 via yeast display and flow cytometry with detergent-solubilized cell lysate. Top variants discovered from this campaign yielded affinities of 8.4 and 11 nM, with the most performant variant, named βm.1, resulting in 1.2 ± 0.2 nM affinity. βm.1 had four β-sheet mutations relative to parental and Tm,app ≥91 °C, with reversible unfolding. The lead variant, βm.1, putatively engages B7-H3 at the same domain I epitope as the parental lead but with improved engagement via a T27F mutation and three homologous mutations. βm.1 is a hyperstable, high affinity miniprotein B7-H3 binder with compelling potential for radioligand therapy and multispecific applications.

item.title: T Cell Receptor-Engineered T Cell Therapy in Solid Tumors: Where We Stand and What's to Come.
item.abstract: T cell receptor-engineered T (TCR-T) cell therapy has emerged as a promising adoptive cellular therapy for solid tumors by enabling recognition of intracellular antigens presented via human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules. Unlike chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy, TCR-T cell therapy targets a broader antigen repertoire, including cancer-testis antigens, neoantigens, and viral antigens. Recent clinical advances, highlighted by the approval of afamitresgene autoleucel in synovial sarcoma, demonstrate meaningful antitumor activity. However, several limitations remain, including HLA restriction, antigen heterogeneity, toxicity related to on-target/off-tumor effects, and mechanisms of resistance such as antigen loss and T cell exhaustion. Advances in antigen selection, gene editing, and synthetic biology are improving both safety and efficacy. Combination strategies and next-generation engineered constructs are expected to overcome current barriers. This review summarizes the biological rationale, clinical evidence, safety considerations, and resistance mechanisms of TCR-T cell therapy in solid tumors and discusses future directions to optimize their therapeutic potential.

item.title: A Simulation-Free Topological Basis for Building Compact Koopman Models of Protein Folding.
item.abstract: Unravelling protein-folding mechanisms and kinetics is a key challenge to biochemical science. The variational approach for Markov processes (VAMP) is a powerful tool to build Markov Models that capture key kinetic and structural information despite the conformational complexity and long time scales associated with protein folding. However, VAMP-based Markov models use data from exhaustive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to construct an underlying basis set describing the "coarse-grained" kinetics; the same MD data can be used to predict transition probabilities between partitioned configuration space, enabling the extraction of folding time scales and mechanism. Here, we propose an alternative strategy for Markov model construction that does not rely on extensive, computationally demanding MD data for configuration space partitioning. Specifically, we show that graph-driven sampling (GDS) can generate a complete "landscape" of intermediate contact-maps linking unfolded and folded protein conformations; importantly, extensive MD simulations are not required in GDS. When combined with a physically intuitive shortest-contact-hop metric to discriminate different intermediate states, GDS mapping of protein-folding configuration space generates a reliable "structurally aware" partitioning for VAMP model construction. To demonstrate this strategy, we show that a GDS-constructed Markov model variationally improves folding time scale estimates for all-atom models of the WW domain protein─and has the additional advantage of easily resolving kinetic traps in the folding landscape that have proven challenging to confirm otherwise. Together, the combination of GDS and VAMP opens a new route toward rapid characterization of protein-folding intermediates and kinetics traps to help address frontier challenges such as protein misfolding, aggregation, and protein design.

item.title: A nanoengineered MSC therapeutic for synergistic therapy of lupus nephritis via cfDNA clearance and targeted immunomodulation.
item.abstract:
RATIONALE: Lupus nephritis (LN) remains a clinical challenge due to the dose-limiting toxicity of conventional immunosuppressants and the poor engraftment/efficacy of mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) therapies.
METHODS: We report a novel nanoengineered MSC therapeutic for LN by engineering MSCs with a cell-free DNA (cfDNA)-targeting dendritic nanogel. To obtain the hybrid MSC-G3K@T system, we coupled tacrolimus-loaded, disulfide-crosslinked polylysine dendrimer nanogels (G3K@T) onto the MSC membrane. Our system exploits two synergistic targeting strategies: the innate homing capacity of MSCs, plus the specific affinity of the cationic G3K dendrimer for anionic cfDNA, which enriches in inflamed kidneys.
RESULTS: Our system acts through two coordinated actions: the nanogel responds to the oxidative renal microenvironment and releases tacrolimus in a spatiotemporally controlled manner, thereby suppressing T-cell activation. At the same time, it scavenges cfDNA, blocking TLR-mediated pro-inflammatory signaling. Working together with the inherent immunomodulatory functions of MSCs, this dual-action strategy yielded robust efficacy in MRL/lpr mice, including a significant reversal of T-cell dysregulation, restoration of glomerular integrity, and reduction of proteinuria and IgG deposition.
CONCLUSIONS: We propose that MSC-G3K@T offers a promising route to augment cell-based therapies, creating a versatile platform that could be used to treat autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.

item.title: Emerging Strategies for the Preservation of Microorganisms of Biomedical and Environmental Importance.
item.abstract: Microorganisms represent the largest component of global biodiversity and play essential roles in biogeochemical cycling, biomedical innovation, and environmental resilience. However, the majority of microbial diversity remains unexplored or inadequately conserved, which poses a threat to scientific reproducibility, public health, and sustainable bioeconomic development. This review evaluates emerging strategies for conserving microorganisms of biomedical and environmental relevance, emphasizing the preservation of viability, genetic stability, and functional integrity across diverse taxa and microbial communities. Traditional methods, such as cryopreservation and lyophilization, are foundational; they present limitations for extremophiles, strict anaerobes, and complex microbiomes. Recent developments incorporate omics-guided preservation, dry-state technologies, and synthetic biology to improve long-term stability and functional fidelity. Innovations such as next-generation freeze-drying, microbiome-level conservation, and engineered microbial systems enhance storage, transport, and reproducibility while reducing dependence on cold-chain infrastructure. The review further addresses regulatory, ethical, and infrastructural challenges related to global biobanking and equitable access to microbial resources. New frameworks prioritize the conservation of functional microbial assemblages over isolated strains, supporting applications in antimicrobial discovery, advanced biotherapeutics, agriculture, and environmental remediation. Advancing microbial conservation is therefore essential for protecting planetary health, advancing biomedical research, and supporting a resilient, sustainable bioeconomy amid global environmental change.
